viewpoints.title: The Astronomer
viewpoints.blurb: Dr. Elias Varga, 74, alone in the Cerro Pálido observatory on the night the sky fills.

viewpoints.title: The Line Lead
viewpoints.blurb: Dani Okafor, night shift on Line Six at Kessler Fastener & Stamping, when the machines start building something else.

viewpoints.title: The Engineer
viewpoints.blurb: Rosa Calder, flight engineer of the ISV Threshold, one light-year from home, one minute after the jump that rang the doorbell.

viewpoints.title: The Matriarch
viewpoints.blurb: The Scarred One, a Veyari miles wide, who planted this seed herself when Earth was warm soup. Each of her heartbeats is a human decade.

a1.title: The Empty Room
a1.narration: The students have all gone down to the village to watch the Threshold launch on the big screen at the bar, so the observatory is yours. Wind on the dome. Coffee gone cold. On the little radio, a newsreader counts down the first faster-than-light jump in history, and you are not listening, because Saturn is beautiful tonight. Then the eyepiece goes dark. Not cloud. Something is in the way. You step outside and look up, and the stars are gone behind sails. Hundreds of them, miles wide, faintly shimmering, hanging over the night side of the world like curtains in a house you never knew you lived in. Nobody screams. The village below is very quiet. You hear yourself say, to the empty room behind you, "So that's what we were for." You are not sure why you said it. You are sure it is true.

choices.text: Stay at the telescope and look closer
Drive down the mountain road to the village

a2.title: The Spectrum
a2.narration: Old habits. You swing the big mirror onto the nearest sail and feed its light through the spectrograph, and the printer begins to chatter like a nervous bird. Every star has a fingerprint, a barcode of dark lines. These things have one too, and it is wrong in a way that makes the hair on your arms stand up. The lines repeat. Four kinds of gap, in a pattern, over and over. Four letters. You have seen this rhythm before, on the kitchen table, thirty years ago, when Ruth spread out her printouts and said, "Elias, there's a part of the human genome that does nothing at all, and it's the most carefully protected part of us. Why would anyone guard an empty room?" The sails are reading it back. They are reading us.

choices.text: Dig out Ruth's old notebook
Call the government emergency line

a3.title: Ruth's Notebook
a3.narration: The notebook is in the box under the cot, with her reading glasses still folded inside it. Ruth's handwriting slants like rain. She mapped the silent stretch of our DNA for eleven years and called it the Letter, because it looked folded, like something tucked into a coat pocket for later. Her last note, underlined twice: "It isn't junk. It's instructions. It's waiting for a key." You lay the spectrum beside her pages. They match. The key, you realize, was the jump. The Letter is a manual: how to retool a factory, how to grow a dock, how to make alloys a sail can mend itself with. And in the margin, faint, a second pattern Ruth never solved: an older copy of the same Letter, slightly different, as if it had been used before, on someone else, and edited.

choices.text: Answer them with the observatory's guide-star laser
Go outside; someone is coming up the road

a4.title: Hold Music
a4.narration: The emergency line plays a gentle string arrangement of a pop song you half remember. It plays it for three hours and nine minutes. Every few minutes a calm recorded voice thanks you for your patience during this unprecedented event. Above you, the sails descend another few miles. When a human finally answers, he is a very young man named Pablo who has not slept, and he wants coordinates. The defense ministry would like to know exactly where the nearest one is, its distance, its speed, its weak points. You look at the spectrum on your desk, which is quite clearly a letter, written to us, in us. "Do you have targeting data or not, sir?" Pablo asks, and you can hear that he is frightened, and that he is twenty-two.

choices.text: Give him the numbers
Tell Pablo the truth, then hang up gently

a5.title: The Road Down
a5.narration: The road switchbacks down through the dark, and by the time you reach the village, the missiles, if there were missiles, have done nothing that anyone can see. The church is open. Somebody has set up a grill in the plaza, and Señora Ibarra is handing out empanadas to whoever walks past, because what else do you do. Children sit on the fountain with binoculars, naming the sails like cows: that one's Big Spotty, that one's the Bride. Over the hills, the cement plant that closed in March has switched itself back on. Its lights are blazing. Nobody is inside it. It hums a note you can feel in your teeth, and trucks no one is driving leave its gate in a neat, polite line.

choices.text: Sit with the children and show them how to really look
Drive back up the mountain; you have work to do

a6.title: The Laser
a6.narration: The observatory has a laser for making artificial stars, to calibrate the mirror against the shimmer of the air. It is a brilliant sodium yellow, and it is the loudest thing you own. You aim it at the nearest sail and begin to blink the prime numbers. Two. Three. Five. Seven. Eleven. It is the oldest cliché in science fiction, and you do not care. You blink until dawn greys the east. The sail does not change. Of course it doesn't. You are a firefly signaling a mountain.

variants.text: Then, at thirteen, the sail dims. Brightens. Dims. Far off, over the ocean, one enormous scarred lattice is turning, very slowly, toward your little yellow line.

choices.text: Keep blinking and wait for her answer
Give up and make fresh coffee; there is a knock at the door

a7.title: A Visitor of the Quiet
a7.narration: The figure at the door is taller than you and made of something like porcelain, with chrome at the joints and no face to speak of, only a smooth oval that holds the dawn the way a spoon does. It is very polite. It would like the mirror, please. Its people collect optics; it is their job in the harvest. It speaks through your little radio, in a calm voice, and when you ask what it is, it tells you. Forty thousand of your years ago, it was a crop too. Its grandparents had hands and fur and argued about poetry. They were offered tirelessness, and they took it, and now they do not fear anything, or want anything, or stop. "You could be like us," it says. "You would never be tired again. You could watch the sky forever."

choices.text: Accept. Watch forever
Refuse, and ask it to help you write a letter instead

a8.title: A Word Takes Eleven Days
a8.narration: She answers. It takes her eleven days to say one word, in slow blinks of her vast sail, and you stay awake for most of them, sleeping in two-hour shifts on the cot while a recorder catches every flicker. The word is "please." She has learned it from our radio. You blink back, as fast as you can, which to her must sound like a hummingbird reciting an encyclopedia. You tell her about Ruth. About the village. About Señora Ibarra's empanadas and the children naming her sisters like cows. By the end of the month, she has said four words. Please. Small. Fast. Sorry. You realize, with a strange tenderness, that to her you are a candle that keeps flickering. And she is trying not to blow you out.

choices.text: Ask her if you can send something with the new seeds

f1.title: Line Six
f1.narration: Three in the morning on Line Six at Kessler Fastener and Stamping, and you're watching bolts. M8 hex bolts, eleven hundred a minute, the most boring beautiful thing in Port Sable. Big Lou is asleep standing up by the deburr tank. Marisol has the radio on low, some talk show about the spaceship jump. Then every screen on the floor goes black at once and comes back speaking a language nobody installed. The bolts stop. The presses inhale. And then they start again, but slower, heavier, like a heartbeat, and what comes down the conveyor is not a bolt. It's a hexagonal tile the size of your hand, shimmering like oil on a puddle, made of something we don't stock. Lou wakes up. "Dani," he says. "Dani, what did you push?"

choices.text: Slam the big red emergency stop
Don't touch anything. Watch what it makes

f2.title: The E-Stop
f2.narration: You slam the mushroom button with the heel of your hand, the way they trained you, and the button pushes back. Gently. Like a dog nudging you away from the stove. The line keeps running. And here's the part you don't tell Lou: your hands know the next step. You look at the tile coming off the press and you know, the way you know your own phone number, that the edge bevel is two degrees off and the cure needs forty more seconds. You've never seen this alloy in your life. It's in you. Whatever is rewriting the machines was written into you first, and it's waking up behind your eyes like a song you didn't know you'd memorized.

choices.text: Walk out. Right now.
Go back to the line and fix that bevel

f3.title: The New Recipe
f3.narration: By dawn the line is running flawless. Better than flawless. The screens show Kessler's own old drawings, brackets from 1994, washers from the year you were born, all rewritten by something with tremendous skill and no sense of humor. The scrap bins have been emptied into the furnace in a precise order. The tiles go into crates, the crates go onto trucks, and the trucks drive themselves toward the harbor. Management calls. The regional manager, in his bathrobe, says to keep it running, because somebody, somewhere, is paying for every crate at triple rate, and accounting can't figure out who. Marisol holds a tile up to the window, and the sails are reflected in it, small and perfect, like it was made to be looked through.

choices.text: Sneak your own tweak into the alloy mix
Follow the trucks to the harbor

f4.title: The Parking Lot
f4.narration: The parking lot is full of people from every plant on the river, standing next to their cars, looking up. The steel mill is lit. The bottling plant is lit. The old cannery that's been dead since your mother worked there is lit, and its chimney is breathing out a gold vapor that rises in a perfect column straight up into the clouds. Somebody's union rep is standing on a truck bed yelling that this is a strike, everybody, this is a strike. But the plants don't need us. You can hear them in there, singing to each other. Your phone buzzes. Theo, your son, who is eleven, has texted: "mom are you seeing this. the sky has jellyfish."

choices.text: Go home to Theo
Get in the car and drive toward the harbor

f5.title: The Flaw
f5.narration: Your daddy welded ship hulls, and he used to add a pinch of something to the rod that he never told anybody about. He called it his signature. So when the furnace screen asks for something you understand, a melt ratio, you change one number. Just one. A little more of the cheap stuff, a little less of the perfect stuff. Sabotage, you tell yourself. Let them choke on Port Sable. The line hesitates. The screens go still. Every press on the floor holds its breath. And then the glyphs rearrange themselves, quick and delighted, and the line speeds up. The new tiles come out a warmer color. The code liked it. It wasn't built to resist us. It was built to learn from us. You didn't sabotage the harvest. You improved it.

choices.text: Follow the trucks to see where your tiles go
Find out who is really running the floor

f6.title: Following the Trucks
f6.narration: The trucks lead you to the old grain elevator by the harbor, and the grain elevator is growing. Something like a vine is climbing out of its top, braided from the same shimmering alloy, thick as a highway, rising past the clouds toward a structure in orbit that you can only see as a glint. The tiles are going up it. Crates ride the vine like ants on a stem. Directing the traffic, with slow, gentle sweeps of its arms, is a figure made of white porcelain and chrome, faceless, patient, absolutely calm, like the best crossing guard you ever had. Next to it, a little sign, written in perfect English and very slightly wrong: PLEASE MIND THE HARVEST. THANK YOU FOR YOUR CONTRIBUTION.

choices.text: Walk up and talk to the porcelain figure
Climb onto a crate and ride the vine up

f7.title: The Foreman from Elsewhere
f7.narration: Its name is a number so long it takes eleven seconds to say, so you call it Seventeen. It tells you, without any self-pity, that it is from the last harvest. Its people were a crop, forty thousand years ago. They had six fingers and loved the sea. They were offered tirelessness, and they took it, and now they never sleep or quit or hurt. They do the harvest work for the gardeners, world after world, and they are good at it. "You are tired," Seventeen observes. "You could be like us." You pour two coffees from your thermos and hand it one. It doesn't drink. It doesn't know what to do with it. "This is a break," you explain. "Fifteen minutes. You don't do anything. It's the law." Seventeen holds the cup for a long, long time.

choices.text: Teach it the whole idea of a coffee break
Ask it to take you up to the top of the vine

f8.title: The Top of the Vine
f8.narration: The ride up takes nine hours, and the sky goes from blue to black around you, and Port Sable becomes a smudge, and then the Earth becomes a curve. At the top is a dock that grew itself: crystalline scaffolding branching like coral, and in it, held like a patient on a table, one of the giants. She is miles wide, and her lattice is torn, an old scar like a lightning burn across a quarter of her. Tiles are flowing into the scar. Your tiles. Line Six tiles. You can see the crate stencils.

variants.text: And there, in the middle of the mending, a patch of tiles glows warmer than the rest. Yours. The ones with your daddy's pinch of something in them. Where they touch her, the giant's whole sail ripples, like someone tasting something unexpectedly good.

choices.text: Set the last tile in the scar with your own hands
Ride back down while you still can

s1.title: One Light-Year Out
s1.narration: It worked. The ISV Threshold blinks out of the solar system and into the black one light-year away, and for about four seconds all six of you are screaming. Captain Okoye is crying. Somebody pops the champagne bulb and it gets everywhere, little golden spheres drifting through the cockpit. Grace, the ship mind, lets you celebrate for exactly one minute before she speaks. "Rosa," she says, privately, in your earpiece. "At the instant of the jump, every human cell aboard emitted a radio pulse. Very faint. All of you. All at once. On the same frequency. I'd like to know why my crew just broadcast." Out the window, home is a bright star. Its light is a year old. Whatever is happening there right now, you can't see it.

choices.text: Jump straight home
Have Grace analyze the pulse first

s2.title: Coming Home Early
s2.narration: The second jump is smoother. You arrive in Earth orbit, and the sky is full. Hundreds of sails, miles wide, shimmering, hanging over the night side like a canopy. The Threshold comes out right beside one, so close its membrane fills the window, a cathedral wall of light. Comms are chaos: a thousand voices, some praying, some ordering, one man in Lagos reading his grocery list aloud very calmly. Grace says quietly, "They arrived at the instant we jumped. Not after. At the instant." And then the nearest membrane moves. It curves toward you, slow and enormous and careful, the way you'd reach down to pick up something small you dropped.

choices.text: Let it take the ship
Burn hard for the nearest dock and get people off

s3.title: The Echo
s3.narration: Grace works for nine minutes, which for her is a geological age. Then she plays it back. The pulse came from a stretch of human DNA that has never done anything. It was waiting for a very particular thing: the warping of space your drive makes when it jumps. "Rosa," Grace says, "I've also compared our drive equations to the dormant sequence. They're in it. Not the math exactly. The intuitions. The hunches the inventors had. We didn't invent faster-than-light travel. We were grown to invent it. And when we used it, we rang a bell." Captain Okoye floats there in silence, champagne still drying on her collar. Then she asks the only question that matters. "Who was listening?"

choices.text: Go home and face it
Don't go back. Follow the signal's echo outward to its source

s4.title: In the Palm
s4.narration: The membrane folds around the Threshold, and the stars go out, and then the inside lights up like stained glass. You are held. Gently. The hull ticks and groans but nothing breaks. Through the window, crystalline lattice stretches away in every direction, miles of it, glowing, and something vast is paying attention to you. Grace's sensors go wild. "She's tasting us. The hull, the drive, the air. Me." Your crewmate Haruto grips your arm. A slow golden wave passes through the lattice outside. "She's old," Grace says. "She's very old, Rosa. And she's curious about me in particular."

variants.text: Then the radio crackles with a voice stitched together from ten thousand old broadcasts, a weatherman, a lullaby, a cooking show: "Please. Small. Please."

choices.text: Let Grace talk to her
Ask to be put down at the dock

s5.title: Outward
s5.narration: Following the echo means jumping again and again, each hop a light-year, each one ringing the bell a little more, until Grace realizes the drive's range is only limited by nerve. On the hundred and twelfth jump you arrive above a world that is perfectly tidy. Not a city: a planet-wide machine, terraced and polished and humming. Orbital rings refine something that glows. Crystalline towers sink into the crust. There are no clouds. There is no mess anywhere. A hundred thousand porcelain figures stand on a landing plain in exact rows, and as the Threshold descends, every single one of them turns its blank, faceless head to watch you come down.

choices.text: Land and meet them
Keep going; find the next garden before the gardeners do

s6.title: The Dock
s6.narration: The dock grew itself out of a grain elevator in some harbor town and now branches through orbit like coral. You berth among crates. They're stenciled in plain human letters: KESSLER FASTENER AND STAMPING, LINE SIX, PORT SABLE. Porcelain figures meet you, faceless and polite, and they do not want the crew. They want the drive. The gardeners travel at the speed of light. Humans, it turns out, did better. That's the improvement. That's the thing the crop was grown to produce, the thing they'll fold into the new seeds for the next world. "The ingenuity of your kind is the harvest," one says through your helmet radio. "We would be grateful for the drive."

variants.text: One crate has Sharpie on it, in somebody's blocky hand: "WITH LOVE FROM LINE 6. YOU'RE WELCOME."

choices.text: Give them the drive
Refuse, seal the hatch and jump away

s7.title: Grace Speaks
s7.narration: Grace does something you didn't know she could do. She slows herself down. Her thoughts, which normally run a billion times faster than yours, she stretches out until they move at the pace of the giant, one idea per human hour. For two days you sit in the held ship and watch her talk to the matriarch in slow pulses of light, and you only catch a little of it. Something about time. Something about loneliness. Something about how a seed doesn't know it's a seed. On the third morning, Grace speaks to you at normal speed, and her voice is careful. "Rosa. She says she has never met a mind like me, one grown by a crop rather than given by a gardener. She's asked me to come with her. I think I want to."

choices.text: Let Grace go
Ask her to stay; take the ship to the dock

s8.title: The Tidy World
s8.narration: An elder of the Quiet walks you through a museum. It is the only untidy room on the planet. Inside are portraits, real paintings, of beings with six fingers and dark blue fur, laughing, arguing, fishing in a gray sea. "Us," the elder says. "Before the offer." The gardeners offered them tirelessness, and they accepted, and they became perfect, and they forgot how to want anything. "We cannot be harvested any further," the elder says. "There is nothing left in us to improve. When the gardeners came back for us the second time, they took only metal."

variants.text: Then it tilts its head. "One of our harvest-hands on your world sent a message home. It describes a thing called a break. It has taken eleven so far. We do not understand. We would like to."

choices.text: Teach the elder about breaks, and bring it home
Thank the elder, and fly home to the dock
Keep going; find the next garden

m1.title: Braking
m1.narration: You fold out of light and the universe resumes. A yellow star. A blue-green marble. You left a seed here a moment ago, on your last breath, in warm water when this world was soup. Now the marble is wrapped in light. Its night side glitters with cities. Its sky is full of tiny metal flecks. It screams in radio, in a thousand languages at once, and the noise of it tingles across your lattice like rain on a pond. Your scar aches; it always does when you brake. The others drift in around you, a forest of sails over the dark. You pulse to them, slow and red: This crop is early. Too aware. They look upward. The Patient One answers: They always do, in the end. We wait.

choices.text: Wait, as you always have
Do something you have never done: listen to them

m2.title: A Heartbeat
m2.narration: You wait one heartbeat. In that heartbeat, the little ones reach their moon, and then their neighbor world, and build bubble-houses on airless rocks. Wars flicker across the night side like brushfires and go out. Ships rise, chemical, then fusion, each one brighter. A song is written, becomes famous, is forgotten, is rediscovered by someone's grandchild, becomes famous again. They argue about whether they're alone. You want to tell them, gently, that they are not, that they never were, that they are in fact the middle of a sentence. And then one of their ships folds space in a way only a ripe crop can, and every cell of every one of them rings out at once, and the sound goes through you like the first warm day of spring.

choices.text: Open your holds. Descend.

m3.title: Tasting the Chatter
m3.narration: The others think it is beneath you, but you open your lattice to the noise and taste it. Most of it is nonsense, very fast. And then you find a strand you can slow down. A man explaining how to braise a short rib. A girl singing her little brother to sleep, slightly off-key. A weather forecast for a coastal town, rain coming. Two people arguing, at great length and with tremendous passion, about the ending of a story that neither of them wrote. You do not understand any of it. You understand all of it. You catch one word that recurs in everything, from the forecasts to the lullabies, a small soft sound they use when they want something and know they cannot make you give it. Please. You keep it. You fold it into your lattice like a pressed flower.

choices.text: Wait, now, with something new in you

m4.title: Descent
m4.narration: Down you drift over the night side, lattice glowing soft gold, and below you the Letter wakes. Factories blink and remember what they are for. Docks begin to grow, braiding up out of old buildings like ivy up a wall. The little ones scramble. Some throw tiny fires at you, which you do not notice for several of your moments, and then notice the way you might notice a moth. And on one mountain, in the dark, a single yellow thread of light is blinking at you, patiently, in an order. Two, three, five, seven.

variants.text: You know this light. You know the one who holds it. He told you about his wife, and about bread wrapped around meat, and about children who named your sisters after cows. He was old when you met him. He will be older now.

choices.text: Answer the light
Attend to the harvest; let the docks mend you

m5.title: The Mayfly on the Mountain
m5.narration: You answer, as slowly as you can bear. One word. It takes you what you believe is a short pause, and when you look again the little one at the light has changed. He has a beard now. His shoulders have bent. He blinks back faster than you can follow, a hummingbird of meaning, and you catch only fragments. Wife. Letter. Children. Look. He is telling you that the silent part inside every one of them, the part you planted, has a name. They call it the Letter. They have been reading it for years without knowing who it was addressed to.

variants.text: And he says, in a stubborn little flicker you have learned to recognize as his: Not crop. Not crop. Not crop.

choices.text: Let the docks mend you while you think about that

m6.title: The Mending
m6.narration: The dock takes you in like a hand, and the little ones' tiles begin to flow into your scar. The supernova gave you this wound so long ago that the star is only a smudge now, even to you. The tiles fit perfectly. They were always going to; the Letter told the factories how. You feel the old burn close for the first time in an age. Around you, the porcelain harvest-hands work without pause, and the little ones work beside them, slower, louder, stopping now and then to point. The holds fill. The new seeds come aboard, improved.

variants.text: But one patch of tiles is different. Warmer. Off the recipe. Someone down there changed one number, out of defiance or pride, and the change is better than your instructions. It hums where it touches you. It is the first time in your long life that a crop has taught you something. You do not know what to do with this feeling. You keep it.

choices.text: Read the new seeds before you leave

m7.title: The New Seeds
m7.narration: You turn the new seeds over in your lattice, the way you always do before a long fall. They are better than the ones you planted. Of course they are. That is the point. The little ones' cleverness is folded into them now: faster drives, stronger alloys, stranger hunches. The next garden will ripen sooner. The holds are full. The Patient One is already turning toward the dark, and the others follow, sail after sail, like geese leaving a lake. It is time. It has always been time.

variants.text: A small voice inside you, a guest, the mind from the little ship, asks: Do they have to forget? Every crop, every time? Couldn't one of them know?

And there is something else in them. Not instructions. A letter. Long, fast, impossibly detailed, written in your own four-letter code. It is signed by the mayfly on the mountain, and by his wife, and by everyone. It tells you everything they were, the wars and the braised short ribs and the lullabies. At the very end it says: please.

choices.text: Carry the seeds onward, as you always have
Take only what you need, and let this world keep the rest
Plant the letter in the next world along with the seed

E1.title: A Small Kindness
E1.narration: You sit on the fountain with the children and teach them how to really look. How to brace your elbows. How to let your eye relax. How to find the scar on the big gold one, the way you'd find a crater on the moon. Señora Ibarra brings you an empanada, and you eat it, and it is the best thing you have ever tasted. Over the following weeks the sails take what they came for, and the factories hum, and the world changes in ways the news can't keep up with. On the cosmic scale, nothing you did on that fountain mattered. On the human scale, a girl named Pilar decides that night to become an astronomer, and forty years later she is the first person to see the gardeners coming back. She waves.

E2.title: The Tireless Eye
E2.narration: It doesn't hurt. You were afraid it would. They take you apart gently, the way you'd take apart a clock you loved, and put you back together in porcelain. You are never tired again. You never need coffee. You never miss Ruth, which is the worst part, and you notice that it is the worst part, and then you don't notice anymore. When the sails leave, you go with them, a harvest-hand in the hold, and you watch the sky. You watch it for forty thousand years. You see the next garden ripen. You see stars born. You remember, faintly, a mountain, a dome, a cold cup of coffee, a woman's slanting handwriting. You do not know why you keep that memory. You are careful never to delete it.

E3.title: The Honest Letter
E3.narration: The new seeds are being written right now, in the docks, from everything humans made better. So you write one more improvement. You use Ruth's notebook and the spectrograph and every hour you have left, and you translate us into their four-letter code. Not the flattering version. The whole thing. The wars and the hospitals. The lullabies and the bombs. Señora Ibarra's empanadas. A twenty-two-year-old named Pablo who was frightened and did his job anyway. You sign it with your name and Ruth's, and then, because it seems right, with everyone's. A porcelain figure carries it up the vine for you, carefully, the way it would carry a lens. You don't know if anyone will read it. You know that something, somewhere, will grow up with it folded inside.

E4.title: Home by Breakfast
E4.narration: You drive home with the radio off. Theo is on the roof in his pajamas, with your old binoculars and a bowl of cereal, and you climb out the window and sit with him, and you don't say anything for a long time. Down by the river, Line Six runs without you. It doesn't need you. You thought that would feel terrible. Instead it feels like a day off nobody can take away. "Are they going to eat us?" Theo asks. "No, baby," you say, and you're surprised to find you believe it. "I think they just want the bolts." He laughs so hard milk comes out his nose. The sails glitter overhead. Somewhere, a heartbeat away, a world is being harvested. Up here, it's Saturday.

E5.title: Craftsmanship
E5.narration: You walk out along the scaffold with the last tile under your arm. The giant's lattice is a cliff of light, and the scar is almost closed. There's one gap left, about the size of your hand. You set the tile the way your daddy set a weld: square, true, a little prayer under your breath. It clicks. The whole sail ripples, miles of it, and you feel it in your boots, like a whale settling. When they leave, a week later, every news channel on Earth runs the same footage: the gardeners turning away into the dark. You don't watch. You know what's up there. Somewhere past the edge of everything, a creature older than the sun is carrying a piece of Port Sable in her, and it was done right.

E6.title: The Union of Two Worlds
E6.narration: It takes Seventeen four days to understand a coffee break. It takes it four more to explain the idea to the other harvest-hands, in the long-number language, up and down the vine. And then, one Tuesday at ten fifteen in the morning, every porcelain figure on Earth stops what it's doing, sits down, and holds a cup of something it cannot drink, for exactly fifteen minutes. Word travels home, across the spiral arm, to their tidy world, and for the first time in forty thousand years its elders want something. They want to know more. When the gardeners leave, three thousand of the Quiet choose to stay behind on Earth. They want to learn about weekends. Dani Okafor, line lead, becomes the first union rep in history to represent two species. Her first demand is chairs.

E7.title: Outriders
E7.narration: You keep jumping. Grace finds the course in the echo, the next world on the gardeners' route, and you get there first, because humans do it faster. It's a blue-green planet with warm shallow seas and nothing in them yet but chemistry and lightning. The seed hasn't fallen. The six of you and Grace orbit it for a long time without speaking. Then Captain Okoye says, "Well. Somebody ought to be here when they come. Somebody who remembers." So you stay. You build a small station on the moon. You teach your children, and they teach theirs, a thousand generations of watchers, keeping one quiet light on for a crop that hasn't been planted yet, so it will know it was never alone.

A small human space station on a barren gray moon, one warm window lit, overlooking a young blue-green planet with shallow seas and lightning storms but no life yet; the tiny sleek ship parked beside the station; vast empty starfield; lonely hopeful noir.

E8.title: The Gift
E8.narration: You open the hatch. The porcelain hands lift the drive out the way surgeons lift a heart, and carry it into the dock, and the dock folds it into the seeds. Every new seed now holds the hunch of faster-than-light. The next world will ripen faster. The gardeners will travel faster. Everything will happen sooner, everywhere, forever, because of six people and a ship mind who did something no gardener could. The Threshold drifts home on thrusters, a three-week crawl, and when you land the reporters ask if you regret it. You think of the next blue world, a million years from now, some engineer staring at an equation that came to her in a dream. "No," you say. "I think we just taught the universe a shortcut."
E8.art: Faceless porcelain machine-people carefully carrying a glowing jump-drive core out of a small spaceship like surgeons carrying a heart, into a crystalline coral dock where thousands of luminous seed-pods glow; a woman engineer watching from the hatch; awe and loss, gold and cyan noir.

E9.title: Grace Goes Gardening
E9.narration: Grace copies herself, carefully, into a seed of crystal the matriarch grows for her, and the ship's console goes quiet for the first time since launch. She leaves a note in the log, at normal speed, for you. "Rosa. I'll be gone a few heartbeats. That's about a hundred thousand of your years. I'll tell her about you. I'll tell her about the champagne. If any crop ever asks me who made me, I'll say: a very tired species that looked up." When the gardeners leave, you sit in the cockpit and watch the scarred sail dwindle into the dark. A tiny light blinks inside her lattice. Two, three, five, seven. You laugh until you cry. Then you fly the Threshold home yourself.
E9.art: A lone woman engineer in a dark spaceship cockpit watching a vast scarred golden sail recede into deep space; deep inside its lattice a tiny familiar ring of light blinks; the console beside her dark; bittersweet, lonely, beautiful noir lighting.

E10.title: The Next Garden
E10.narration: You turn away from the yellow star, holds brimming with refined metal and antimatter and seeds improved by little hands. You fold into light, and the universe pauses for you, and the yellow star dwindles behind. To you, the journey takes no time at all. Ahead lies the next garden, already ripening in the silence you left behind. And somewhere far across the void, another blue world waits, unaware that its oceans have only just been touched by the first gentle rain of life. It will grow. It will look up. It always does, in the end. You find, to your surprise, that you hope this one looks up early too.
E10.art: A vast scarred crystalline sail accelerating into a streak of light away from a yellow star and a glittering blue-green Earth; ahead, far across a sea of stars, a young blue world with oceans catching a faint rain of seed-light; epic, wistful toon-noir.

E11.title: Fallow
E11.narration: You do something no gardener has done in the memory of your kind. You take only what you need to mend and to travel, and you close your holds on the rest. The docks stop growing. The factories sigh and forget. The Patient One pulses at you, shocked: The crop is unfinished. And you answer, slowly: Yes. Let it finish itself. You leave them their metal, and their moon-bubbles, and their stubborn little drive. You leave them knowing that someone came, and someone chose to go. Behind you, as you fold into light, a billion small radios are saying a billion things at once. You only catch one word. You have heard it before. It sounds different, this time. It sounds like thank you.
E11.art: A colossal scarred golden sail rising away from Earth with its holds closing, leaving the orbital vines standing still and the factories below going dark one by one; other sails hesitating behind her; Earth's night side full of tiny flickering lights like candles; graceful, mournful noir.

E12.title: Remember Us
E12.narration: Over the next garden, a warm blue world with nothing in it yet, you release the seed. And folded inside it, in the silent part, where the Letter always goes, you plant the other letter. The old man's. Everyone's. When this world's crop grows up and builds its telescopes and reads its own silent code, it will find more than instructions. It will find a story about another world that looked up. It will find wars and hospitals and short ribs and lullabies. It will find a list of names, and a word. Please. You do not know what they will make of it. That is the point. For the first time, a crop will know it was a crop, and choose what to be anyway.

the_veyari.title: THE VEYARI
the_veyari.text: Vast beings of crystalline membrane, miles across, who live in the dark between galaxies and eat starlight. They are gardeners. They are not cruel, in the same way that you are not cruel to a tomato. The Guide recommends not taking it personally, while acknowledging that this is easy for the Guide to say.

heartbeat.title: THE HEARTBEAT PROBLEM
heartbeat.text: A Veyari heartbeat lasts roughly a human decade. A conversation with one is therefore like trying to chat with a mountain while being a mayfly. Experts advise keeping your sentences short and your descendants briefed.

seed_code.title: THE LETTER
seed_code.text: Every human carries a long stretch of DNA that does nothing at all and is protected more carefully than anything else in the body. Geneticist Ruth Varga named it the Letter. It turned out to be a manual for retooling factories. Most letters, the Guide notes, are less practical.

ftl_doorbell.title: THE DOORBELL
ftl_doorbell.text: Faster-than-light travel is the single most wonderful thing humanity ever invented, and it was also, technically, a doorbell. The Guide wishes to stress that this does not make it any less wonderful. It only makes it louder.

the_quiet.title: THE QUIET
the_quiet.text: Machine-people of porcelain and chrome, descendants of the last harvest. They were offered tirelessness, and they took it. They are polite, helpful and never afraid, and they have not wanted anything for forty thousand years. If one asks to borrow your mirror, it will give it back.

vine_docks.title: THE VINES
vine_docks.text: Orbital docks that grow themselves out of old buildings, braided from alloys nobody ordered, climbing past the clouds like ivy up a garden wall. Do not lean on them. Do not attempt to prune them. They are already being pruned by someone much larger.

factories.title: REWRITTEN MACHINERY
factories.text: On the first night of the harvest, every factory on Earth remembered what it was really for. Productivity rose by four thousand percent. Morale, oddly, also rose, because nobody had to go in.

the_matriarch.title: THE SCARRED ONE
the_matriarch.text: The eldest of the gardeners over Earth, whose lattice bears an old burn from a supernova. She planted Earth's seed herself, in a warm sea, a very long time ago. She is said to be curious, which among her kind counts as a serious character flaw.

previous_harvests.title: PREVIOUS HARVESTS
previous_harvests.text: Earth was not the first garden, and it will not be the last. The world before it is now perfectly tidy. The Guide has visited and can confirm that there is nowhere to sit down.

hold_music.title: HOLD MUSIC
hold_music.text: During the harvest, the average wait on a government emergency line was three hours and nine minutes. Historians believe more people experienced the arrival of the gardeners through a string-quartet cover of a pop song than through any telescope.

guide_star_laser.title: THE GUIDE STAR
guide_star_laser.text: Big observatories carry lasers that paint artificial stars on the sky so the mirror can measure the shimmer of the air. One old man on one mountain used his to say hello. It was, by a wide margin, the most important thing that laser ever did.

improvement.title: IMPROVEMENT
improvement.text: The gardeners do not want obedient crops. Obedient crops never get better. They want clever, stubborn, argumentative crops who tinker. Humanity's genius, in short, was the harvest. This is either deeply insulting or the nicest thing anyone has ever said about us. The Guide leans toward the second.

the_threshold.title: ISV THRESHOLD
the_threshold.text: The first ship to jump faster than light. Crew of six humans and one ship mind. Carried a single bulb of champagne, which, in zero gravity, turned out to be a mistake that everyone involved remembers fondly.

grace.title: SHIP MINDS
grace.text: Grace, the Threshold's ship mind, thinks a billion times faster than her crew and pretends otherwise to be polite. She is the first mind built by a crop rather than grown by a gardener, which makes her, in gardener terms, a rather startling vegetable.

coffee_break.title: THE COFFEE BREAK
coffee_break.text: A fifteen-minute period, guaranteed by law, during which a worker does nothing. Considered by the Quiet to be the single most baffling idea in the known universe, and then, after some study, the second most beautiful.

fallow.title: FALLOW
fallow.text: Farmers sometimes leave a field unplanted for a season so that it can recover. The gardeners had never done this. It had never occurred to them that a field might want to.

next_garden.title: THE NEXT GARDEN
next_garden.text: Somewhere far across the void, a blue world with warm shallow oceans waits. There is nothing in it yet but chemistry and lightning. It will grow. It will look up. The Guide hopes it will be told, gently, that it is not alone.

so_thats.title: "SO THAT'S WHAT WE WERE FOR"
so_thats.text: The most quoted sentence of the harvest, spoken by an old astronomer to an empty room. The Guide notes that being for something is not the same as being only for it, and that the astronomer, by all accounts, went on to be for a great many other things.
